title: Phillies vs. Braves Game 3 Wild Card FAQ: Time, Channel, Odds & What to Expect (8 ET)
body:
The National League Wild‑Card showdown reaches a decisive third game on Tuesday night, with the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies set to clash in an 8 p.m. ET contest that could send one club into the postseason while ending the other’s hopes. After the Braves rallied to steal Game 1 and the Phillies answered with a dramatic comeback in Game 2, both teams arrive in Atlanta with their backs against the wall, and every managerial decision, bullpen matchup and defensive nuance will be magnified under the bright lights of Truist Park.

Game 3 will be broadcast on NBC and streamed on Peacock, and the broadcast crew has already outlined the key storylines that will shape the outcome. Starting pitcher Bryce Harper’s replacement, Aaron Nola, will take the mound for Philadelphia, while the Braves will counter with rookie right‑hander Dylan Dodd, who earned his first postseason start after a strong showing in the regular season. Both pitchers have been effective this year—Nola posted a 2.78 ERA over 180 innings, while Dodd posted a 3.12 ERA in 140 innings—but the pressure of a winner‑takes‑all scenario could expose any lingering inconsistencies, particularly Dodd’s tendency to miss his spots deep in the middle innings.

The bullpens will likely be the decisive factor. Atlanta’s closer, A.J. Minter, has been a revelation this postseason, recording two saves and striking out 13 batters in 9 ⅔ innings. He will be available for a potential ninth‑inning showdown if the game remains tight. Philadelphia, on the other hand, will rely on veteran reliever Craig Kimbrel, who returned from a brief injury layoff to post a 2.25 ERA in his last three regular‑season appearances. The Phillies also have a deep pool of left‑handed arms, including Ranger Suarez and Nick Pivetta, who could be called upon to neutralize the Braves’ power‑hitting core—particularly the left‑handed slugger Ronald Acuña Jr., who has already logged three home runs in the series.

Off the field, the series has reignited a bitter rivalry that dates back decades, with both clubs vying for dominance in the NL East. Atlanta’s front office has emphasized the need to protect its young talent, especially the high‑priced contracts of Acuña and Ozzie Albies, while Philadelphia’s front office is looking to prove that its recent roster overhaul—highlighted by the acquisition of Bryce Harper and the emergence of rookie sensation Spencer Turnbull—has finally translated into postseason success. The psychological edge also leans toward the Phillies, who have never lost a Game 2 after dropping the first, but the Braves have a history of rallying in elimination games, as evidenced by their Game 1 comeback.

Statistically, the series is balanced. Both teams have posted a .260 batting average in the two games, while the Braves have outscored the Phillies 10‑9 on the strength of timely extra‑base hits. However, the Phillies hold a slight advantage in on‑base percentage (OBP .340 vs. .332), and their baserunning aggression could force errors from a Braves defense that has struggled with double plays all season. The key will be which club can capitalize on scoring opportunities in the early innings; a two‑run lead by the third inning has historically translated into a 70 % win rate in postseason games.

As the final game of the Wild‑Card series looms, the stakes could not be higher. A victory for Atlanta would propel the Braves into the Division Series, extending their quest for a World Series title that has eluded them since 1995. For Philadelphia, a win would mark a historic breakthrough, validating a multi‑year rebuild and delivering the city its first postseason series win since 2009. Fans can expect a tightly contested duel, with every pitch, hit and defensive play potentially writing the next chapter in one of baseball’s most storied rivalries. The outcome on Tuesday night will not only decide which team moves forward but also set the tone for the remainder of the postseason.
